$comment: Written by tools/buildSeason.ts from tools/season/design.ts; do not hand-edit.

families.focus: Five targets on one level; flick sideways and stop dead.
families.why: Horizontal flicks isolated. Wide Wall and 1w3ts mix both axes, so a player who over-travels sideways and one who under-travels vertically get the same score and no hint which they are.

families.focus: Flick up and down; the sideways movement is only ever a correction.
families.why: Vertical flicks isolated. Of the 58 static clicking scenarios measured with 10,000 or more players, 51 spawn targets over a field wider than it is tall (data/season-1/science.json), so vertical stopping gets the least practice.

families.focus: Small moves, smaller targets; settle the crosshair before you click.
families.why: Micro-correction at close spacing, the skill behind 1w2ts and Raw Mouse Control; RawMouseControlClicking3 is replayed 51.6 times per player (data/fun_audit.json).

families.focus: A wide formation; big flicks across it, in both directions.
families.why: Large-amplitude flicks over a wide two-dimensional field, where Galaga keeps to one line. Targets are larger to keep the index of difficulty in the same range as the rest of the category.

families.focus: Clear the whole constellation; the next one appears when its last star falls.
families.why: Real star patterns as waves - the Big Dipper, the Little Dipper, Orion, Cassiopeia, Cygnus, Leo - seven stars each, so every wave is a route to plan as well as seven flicks to make.

families.focus: Targets at two distances; read the size before you decide how far to move.
families.why: Depth. The far ring is half the angular size of the near one, so the same flick distance asks for two different stopping precisions within one run - and the three targets are three sizes too (0.75x, 1x, 1.35x), so how big a target looks is never only its distance.

families.focus: Six small targets up at once; take the nearest, keep the rhythm.
families.why: The 1wall 6targets shape - the most-played static scenario measured, 1.29 million players (data/fun_audit.json) - at every band, so the category always has a six-target scenario.

families.focus: Six still targets on one wall; take the nearest, keep the rhythm.
families.why: The first Gravity Well as it played: fuglaa's balloons on their own wall with their attack left out, so they stand still - six at a time, a 1wall 6targets on a different field.

families.focus: Slow floaters; match their drift for a moment, then click.
families.why: The entry to moving targets: slow, long-lived paths that reward confirming the shot rather than guessing it. Floating Heads Timing 400% has the most players of any dynamic-clicking scenario in data/fun_audit.json (352,281).

families.focus: Slow swings from wall to wall; click on the swing, not only at the turn.
families.why: A pendulum: slow, straight, level runs that turn only at the walls, so the swing is long and even and the skill is horizontal timing alone. Its movement is Floating Heads Timing 400%'s, slowed down.

exceeds.why: Slower than the slowest of 54 popular dynamic-clicking scenarios (7.45 deg/s) on purpose: the playtest found it too fast from Intermediate up, and asked for it slowed down a lot. Its thresholds are the model reading below the speeds it was fitted on, so they are the first to recut from real runs.

families.focus: Read the arc; the top of the bounce is the slowest moment.
families.why: Gravity arcs. A bot under gravity is the one design feature that goes with both more replay and more reach (Spearman +0.10 and +0.13 over 614 catalogued scenarios): small, but the only positive signal on both.

families.focus: Straight runs up and down, a dead stop at every turn, and a charged-up buzz all the while.
families.why: Linear motion with a vibration on top: the target runs straight up and down, stops dead before it changes direction, and shakes side to side many times a second the whole time - so the stop is the moment to click, and the player reads it through the noise, the micro-adjustment cA 5ts vibrate is played for. Vertical since the playtest: every other moving family already travels sideways. The difficulty model reads a target's speed from its walking speed, which here is the buzz, so it prices every band at the buzz's 10 deg/s and sees only the targets shrinking; calibration from real runs is what corrects that.

exceeds.why: The side-to-side reversal is the buzz, every 0.04 to 0.08 s as cA 5ts vibrate shakes, not a strafe; no popular click scenario vibrates sideways, so none reverses that fast. The travel itself turns every 1.5 to 2.5 s at Novice.

families.focus: Two fast crossers in an open sky; move with the target and click inside the motion.
families.why: High-speed dynamic clicks. Speed is the other axis of difficulty besides size: at the board median the fitted model prices a doubling of angular speed, 20 to 40 degrees a second, at about half a bit of Fitts difficulty (0.55).

families.focus: Straight lines across the sky; lead nothing, match the line and click.
families.why: Linear motion, the Floating Heads idea made exact: every target runs a straight lane from one side of the view to the other and back, level (lanes that rose and fell left the targets pinned to the ceiling in the playtest), so the path is readable at a glance and the only question is timing.

families.focus: Pop them before they reach you; every one that does costs you.
families.why: Speed clicking under pressure, on fuglaa's design: balloons that dash at the player and burst on arrival, so a target left alive costs score rather than only time. The dash takes about 1.7 seconds to arrive at Novice and gets about 1.1x faster each band, and the player has three rounds before a reload, and the game itself runs faster each band too, its timescale up 0.1 a band.

families.focus: Floating heads: big, slow drifters; confirm the shot before you click.
families.why: Voltaic's Floating Heads movement exactly - its own two dodge profiles, untouched - with larger, slower targets, so the most-played floating movement is in the season at a Novice anyone can start on.

families.focus: Fliers in front of you drifting nearer and further as they rise and fall; follow them and click.
families.why: psalmTS's motion as a clicking task: targets strafe round the player on long, even runs while climbing and dropping, linear in each axis and curved together.

families.focus: Long, smooth strafes; ease into each turn with the target.
families.why: Smoothness on the ground. The target accelerates over a third of a second, so its reversals are gentle and following them cleanly is the whole skill.

families.focus: Mostly up and down; keep the crosshair level with it through each turn.
families.why: Vertical smoothness, which ground tracking barely tests. The target flies, turns vertically about as often as it strafes, and strafes slowly.

families.focus: Curves in both directions; follow the path, do not cut its corners.
families.why: Two-axis smooth tracking: horizontal and vertical reversals on similar clocks draw curves rather than lines.

families.focus: A small, slow target; precision over speed.
families.why: Fine control: at this size the tolerance for drift is under a degree, and at this speed there is no excuse for it.

families.focus: Long jumps under low gravity; carry the crosshair along the arc.
families.why: Smooth diagonal tracking: slow strafes combined with floaty jumps, so the path is an arc rather than a line or a zig-zag.

families.focus: A close target sweeping wide that blinks now and then; track it, and find it again after the jump.
families.why: Close range means large angular speed at a modest real speed, the arm-tracking demand Smoothbot and Close Long Strafes are played for; and Ground Plaza's blink, a short teleport, rare at Novice and more frequent every band, so recovery joins smoothness.

families.focus: Close, snappy strafes; react to the turn, do not predict it.
families.why: The close-range strafe duel of Close Fast Strafes (117,749 players, 22.4 plays each, data/fun_audit.json).

families.focus: Strafes and range changes; the target shrinks and grows as it moves.
families.why: Mid-range reactive tracking with forward and back movement, so size and speed change under the player during a strafe.

families.focus: It stops before it turns, and now and then stops dead for a second or two; stop with it.
families.why: Stop-start movement: a pause before each reversal, and every so often a full stop of a second or two, punish the player who keeps moving on momentum, a common reactive-tracking fault.
learnsFrom: Flicker Plaza rAim Easy Less Blinks

families.focus: Jumps and short strafes together; follow it up as well as across.
families.why: Reactive tracking through the air, the pattern of Air Angelic 4, which nine of evxl's listed benchmarks use.

families.focus: A flier changing direction on both axes; react on whichever one moves.
families.why: Three-dimensional reactive tracking: short horizontal and vertical reversals on independent clocks.

families.focus: Being tracked makes it turn; stay on it through the dodge.
families.why: Reactive dodging: the target reverses shortly after it is hit, so the longer a player holds on, the more it tests the recovery rather than the lock.

families.focus: Kill, then move straight to the next; no pause between targets.
families.why: The core speed-switching loop on still targets in a compact field: the time between targets is what the score measures.

families.focus: Switches across a curved wall; land the flick, then hold.
families.why: Speed switching on the curved wall Voltaic's 1w4ts is played on, its map copied whole, where the flick between targets is most of the time spent.

families.focus: Switch up and down; stop on each one before you fire.
families.why: Vertical switching, the axis the rest of the category barely uses.

families.focus: Six small targets packed tight; short, exact moves.
families.why: Precision switching: small targets and small moves, the micro side of speed switching.

families.focus: Slow floaters that fall fast; the switch is the skill, the tracking only has to be clean.
families.why: Speed switching on slow movers, the bridge to evasive switching: EddieTS (185,895 players on its Novice cut) at a gentler pace, with short kills so the switch dominates.

families.focus: Each target takes a while; stay on it to the end, then switch.
families.why: Longer kills on still targets: the discipline of finishing before leaving, which short-kill scenarios never test.

families.focus: Six strafing targets; kill one without losing track of the others.
families.why: The standard evasive-switching problem, targets that move while you are on them and while you are not, at the pace of DriftTS.

families.focus: Clay pigeons thrown across the field; catch each one on its arc.
families.why: Skeet Tracking's own mechanism - targets with no walking speed, thrown sideways and up by a movement ability, falling under gravity. It has the most players of any evasive-switching scenario in data/fun_audit.json (385,771, 31.3 plays each).

families.focus: Fliers sweeping round in curves; pick the next one before this one dies.
families.why: Three-dimensional evasive switching on curved paths: horizontal and vertical reversals on matching clocks with slow acceleration, so each target sweeps round in an arc instead of zig-zagging.

families.focus: Targets heal when left alone; finish every kill you start.
families.why: Regeneration makes leaving early costly: a half-killed target is back to full a second later. Regen Control and tamTargetSwitch are played for exactly this.

families.focus: One tough target; stay on it, and find it again the moment it respawns.
families.why: One evasive target with enough health to take a sustained effort, which respawns somewhere new when it dies: the kill-then-reacquire loop of switching with nothing else on screen to hide behind.

families.focus: Close targets moving fast across the view; stay with them, then turn to the next.
families.why: Close-range evasive switching, where modest real speeds become large angular speeds and every switch is also a tracking catch-up.
